title: What does a consultant actually do all day?
description: A realistic look at a junior consultant's day and week: analysis, slides, client meetings, team problem solving, travel and the hours involved.
hook: Job descriptions talk about "solving clients' toughest problems", which sounds exciting but does not tell you how you would spend a Tuesday. Here is a more honest picture of what junior consultants actually do, including the parts people do not put on recruiting brochures.
body:
A typical week for a junior consultant

  • Analysis. A lot of time goes into spreadsheets: cleaning data, building simple models, testing whether a hypothesis holds up.
  • Interviews. Speaking to the client's staff, customers, suppliers or industry experts to understand what the numbers do not show.
  • Slides. Turning findings into clear charts and messages. Each slide usually has a one-sentence headline that states the insight, much like an action title.
  • Team problem solving. Short sessions with your manager to decide what the findings mean and what to do next.
  • Client meetings. Updating the client team, testing ideas, and presenting progress to senior executives.

Where the work happens

Often at the client's office for part of the week, especially on bigger projects, and in your own office or at home for the rest. Travel varies hugely by firm, office and project. Some consultants travel most weeks; others rarely leave their city.

The hours

Long hours are common, especially before a big presentation. They vary by firm, project and manager. It is worth asking people at each firm how their typical week really looks.

What makes people love it

  • Learning fast: new industries and problems every few months.
  • Working with smart, motivated colleagues.
  • Seeing how senior leaders make decisions, early in your career.
  • Clear feedback and a structured path to grow.

What people find hard

  • Long or unpredictable hours, and travel.
  • Moving on before you see the results of your work.
  • Pressure to perform and be promoted on a set timeline (see the career path).

How this connects to interviews

Every part of a case interview maps to a part of the job: structuring is planning the work, maths is the analysis, charts are reading data, and the recommendation is the final presentation. Practising cases is a small rehearsal of the real thing.

An example week

  • Monday: travel to the client, team planning, interviews with two regional managers.
  • Tuesday: clean the sales data, build a first model of margins by product.
  • Wednesday: problem-solving session with the manager; turn the findings into five draft slides.
  • Thursday: update meeting with the client team, then rework the analysis based on their questions.
  • Friday: work from your home office, finish slides for next week's steering committee.

Every project is different, but the rhythm of analysis, discussion and slides is common.

Sources

  • Hacking the Case Interview: What is management consulting?

Checked November 2026.
